My name is Chinenye Precious Anyasor, and I have a bachelor's in human physiology. By now, I thought I would be working in a lab somewhere, but alas, life had its plans.
These are the tools I used to write, design, and publish my portfolio.

I have been thinking about something lately. When we say “creatives” in Nigeria, we immediately think of the entertainment and fashion industry. That’s it. It’s like we have boxed creativity into just a few visible careers: makeup artists, skit makers, stylists, videographers, directors, musicians. People in the film and fashion space, basically. But I recently watched a documentary on Netflix called Abstract: The Art of Design, and it completely shifted my perspective. There are entire creative worlds I never even considered, never even heard of until now. Stage designers. Footwear designers. Illustrators. Architects. Automobile designers. Technical documentators. People who do not just make things but solve problems with beauty, precision, and intentional design. It blew my mind in a way I still cannot explain. And the sad part is, many of these creative fields actually exist here in Nigeria. But they are: Mostly not understood as creative work, Underfunded, Not documented or celebrated publicly, Or shoved aside in favour of survival-driven trades. Take architecture, for example. We have architects, but they rarely approach the work they produce as their life’s work or legacy; the mindset is usually, “let’s just build a house,” not “let’s design something sustainable or unforgettable.” Same with footwear: it’s “let’s make shoes and sell,” not “let’s create something that solves a pain point, like helping an athlete perform better.” Even stage design: there is barely any talk about it as a career, yet it’s such a brilliant form of art expression. I do not know if it’s a Nigerian issue, a third-world issue, or both, but I genuinely believe our environment limits how far creativity is allowed to go and our career options. Not because the talent is not there, but because there’s little room, support, or even language for it to grow. When survival is the main goal, it’s hard to make space for creativity that’s innovative, bold, or experimental. If you have not seen Abstract Design on Netflix, you really should. It will make you rethink what it even means to be creative and maybe even inspire you to approach your own creativity with fresh eyes.

Introduction​ Nigeria has come a long way with payments. From manual bank payments, where we queued for hours, to early mobile/internet banking, to the rise of online payments that fuelled the explosion of online shopping. You can buy anything online these days, from foodstuff to gadgets, without leaving your home, yet many people don't know how online payments work and often wonder how they work. Well, you are about to find out. To fully understand how online payments work, you need to understand payment service providers, payment gateways, and webhooks.

Nigeria has come a long way with payments. From manual bank payments, where we queued for hours, to early mobile/internet banking, to the rise of online payments that fuelled the explosion of online shopping. You can buy anything online these days, from foodstuff to gadgets, without leaving your home, yet many people don't know how online payments work and often wonder how they work. Well, you are about to find out. To fully understand how online payments work, you need to understand payment service providers, payment gateways, and webhooks.

They are companies that own and provide the technology (payment gateway and payment processor) businesses use to collect payments from customers online. They make it possible for you to shop and pay online. Some of them include: Paystack, Flutterwave, PayU, Seerbit and others.

A payment gateway is the technology that lets a business accept online payments. It securely collects and encrypts a customer’s payment details at checkout, whether by card, bank transfer, or another method, and passes them to the payment processor, which completes the transaction with the customer’s bank. The exact steps through which this happens are a bit complicated and different for each online payment option, but let's look at how a card payment works. Sarah’s clothing vendor is running a website sale. To shop, she opens the website, selects a few items, chooses card payment, enters her card details, and completes the payment. To walk through the process by which the payment gateway ensures Sarah’s payment gets to her vendor, you need to understand the following:​ Encryption: this process secures Sarah’s card details so only the necessary parties can access them. Issuing bank: this is Sarah’s bank; she has an account with them. They issued the debit and credit card whose details she entered during checkout. Payment Processor: the part of the payment service provider that receives encrypted card details from the payment gateway, sends them to the issuing bank for authorization, and returns an approval or decline. Authorization: the process by which Sarah’s bank checks whether she has enough funds in her account for the items she wants to buy and whether her account has any restrictions. Acquiring bank: this is the bank that receives and holds payment made through a debit or credit card on behalf of the payment service provider till they send it to Sarah’s vendor’s account. Settlement: this is when Sarah’s bank moves the required amount from her account to the payment service provider’s bank, called the acquiring bank. Now that we are familiar with these concepts, let’s walk through the simplified version of how a payment gateway ensures that Sarah’s vendor receives her payment.​ The gateway receives Sarah’s card details and encrypts them. The gateway sends the encrypted data to the provider’s payment processor. The payment processor sends an authorization request to the issuing bank (Sarah’s bank). The issuing bank checks Sarah’s account to see whether it has enough funds to cover the items she wants to buy. It also checks that her account isn't frozen or restricted due to fraud. The issuing bank approves or declines the payment based on the results of these checks. The payment processor passes the result back to the gateway, which shows Sarah a message on her screen: “Payment successful” or “Payment failed.” At the same time, the payment service provider sends a webhook to the vendor’s server, so the vendor knows the payment went through and can process Sarah’s order. Later, usually within a day or two, the issuing bank (Sarah’s bank) sends the required amount to the payment service provider’s acquiring bank. This transfer is called settlement. The payment service provider sends the money to Sarah’s vendor’s bank account.

In step 7, we mentioned a webhook. Let’s look at it from the vendor’s perspective. How does Sarah’s vendor find out that her payment was successful? That’s where a webhook comes in. A webhook is an automated message from a payment service provider to the vendor’s server. It is sent when something happens on the provider’s platform that affects the vendor, such as a payment succeeding or failing, a settlement being made, or a refund being issued, among others.
Now you understand the basics of how online payments work, from the role of payment service providers and payment gateways to how webhooks keep businesses informed about transactions.

When you watch people dancing, what are your thoughts? I will tell you what mine usually are. I am thinking this is someone who has decided that joy is more important than looking composed. I am thinking this is someone who has decided not to carry the weight of everyone's opinion, if only for a few minutes. I am thinking this is someone who has permitted themselves to be whimsical. To be childlike. I find it even more fascinating when they are people I know have serious jobs. People who spend Monday to Friday making difficult decisions, leading teams, paying salaries, meeting deadlines. Then the music comes on, and suddenly they are just, well... dancing. There is something beautiful about that. When I dance, I am not thinking about bills that need to be paid or any of the responsibilities that come with my adult life. I am listening to the beat. The lyrics. I am remembering where I first heard that song. I am remembering who I was when I first loved it. And somehow, without thinking too much about it, I trust my body to move however it wants to. I think dancing in front of people is brave. It is brave because you are choosing joy over self-consciousness. You are saying, "I would rather enjoy this moment than spend it wondering how I look." And I think that takes courage. Not everyone has that courage, and that is okay too. I also think the best kind of dancing is dancing with your people. Family. Friends. Or strangers who, for one song, become your people because everyone has decided to stop taking themselves so seriously. I cannot believe I have written this much about dancing. But maybe this is not really about dancing. Maybe it is about giving yourself permission to be free, even if it is only for one song. So dance today. Not because you are good at it. Just because you can.

If you are anything like me, then at some point in your childhood, and maybe even now as an adult, you have probably been called stubborn. Truth be told, before it became a voice, I actually was stubborn. I would refuse to do what I had been told for no reason at all. At least, that's how I choose to see it. But somewhere along the way, something changed. I do not think I am stubborn anymore. I think I just have a voice. The difference is that every decision I make, I can explain. Whether that explanation makes sense to you or not is not something that concerns me. I have thought about it, I have wrestled with it, and I have chosen it. People are not used to that. If I go with my gut even when nobody else understands it, I am called stubborn. If I listen to everyone's opinion and still arrive at a different conclusion, I am called stubborn. If I ask for advice and do not follow it, I am called stubborn. For me, advice has never meant handing over my decision-making to someone else. It has always meant gaining another perspective. That's it. I listen. I think about it. I keep what is useful. I discard what is not. Then I make my choice. But I have realized that not everyone sees advice that way. Some people assume that the moment you ask for their opinion, you have also agreed to follow it. So when you do not, they conclude that you are stubborn. Or maybe you have simply learned to think for yourself. If there's one thing I hope more people develop, it is a voice. When you are confused, quiet yourself long enough to hear what you actually want. Then seek perspectives from people you trust. Listen carefully. Think deeply. And then decide. Do not outsource your decision-making to other people. Sometimes we do it without even realizing it. We look for permission instead of perspective. We keep asking person after person until someone tells us what we wanted to hear all along. Learn to catch yourself. So how do you develop a voice? Spend time alone with your thoughts. Ask yourself questions, even when you do not immediately have the answers. Sit with the discomfort of not knowing. Learn to enjoy your own company. Then read. Books expose you to lives you will never live and experiences you will never have. Sometimes they put words to thoughts you have carried around for years but never knew how to express. They do not tell you what to think; instead, they teach you how to think. Over time, they sharpen your voice. They strengthen your values. And your values become the reference point for the decisions you make. So I will ask you again. Are you stubborn? Or do you simply have a voice?

Meritrade is an online stock trading app owned and controlled by Meristem, used to buy and sell stocks on the Nigerian stock exchange, provide up-to-date market insights, and let users set up a watchlist for stocks of interest so they never miss an opportunity to buy or sell. This guide walks you through the steps required to buy stocks on Meritrade.

I took several technical communication courses and wanted to practice what I learned. I chose an app and created four user guides for Meritrade, a stock-trading platform. They cover: Creating an account Funding an account Buying stocks Selling stocks I also included an FAQ section as part of my unofficial portfolio project.
The guide is written for end users who, regardless of their investing experience, have never used Meritrade and aren't familiar with its user interface (UI).

Identified my users. Researched the product and the workflows I wanted to document by using the product myself. Wrote down my first draft in Markdown in VS Code. Annotated screenshots in Greenshot for the guides. Edited the guides against my style guide built from patterns I caught in my drafts. Version-controlled the guides with Git and published them on GitHub.

Early on, each guide had its own top-level image folder. As the suite grew to four guides, I restructured to a single images/ folder with a subfolder per guide. It’s a small choice, but it helps anyone browsing the repo see one clear system instead of four similar ones. This consistency reflects my goals for the writing and the file structure. I picked ‘stocks’ over ‘shares’ early and used it everywhere, across all four guides. Switching between the two in the middle of a document or suite might confuse readers. They could think the terms mean different things. Using one consistent term removes that doubt. I felt torn between adding an FAQ inside each guide and creating a standalone FAQ section. I chose the latter. I wanted all answers in one place. This way, the task guides stayed short and focused. Plus, it made updating one page easier.

While documenting the workflow for creating a Meritrade account, the phone verification step failed. I was supposed to receive an OTP to verify my phone number, but I didn't. Despite clicking Resend OTP several times, I still didn’t receive the OTP. I contacted the support team, but they didn’t respond that day. So I started the account creation process again, but found I couldn't because the process I started the other day was still active; I just hadn't completed the registration. So instead of clicking on ‘Create account’, I clicked on ‘Login’. Surprisingly, I was no longer stuck on the phone verification step, but I had moved to the next step. (An undocumented workaround). I got stuck again at the last step in the registration process, where I was required to create my 4-digit PIN. For every 4-digit combination I entered, I kept getting an error message that read: 'PIN already exists. Please use Change PIN’. It’s important to note that nowhere on the screen could I click ‘Change PIN’. I contacted the support team; they fixed it, but I never saw the success screen to be able to document how users should know the account creation process is complete or successful, hence why step 8 of the account creation guide is incomplete. It should include a success confirmation. This is a software issue, so the engineering team should handle it, not the support team. The engineering team should either fix it, offer a workaround, or list it as a known issue in the troubleshooting guide.
Four user guides, the style guide, and a consistent folder structure.
Re-test the flow to check if the OTP and PIN issue has been fixed. Update my guides to show the fix.

Meritrade is an online stock trading app owned and controlled by Meristem, used to buy and sell stocks on the Nigerian stock exchange, provide up-to-date market insights, and let users set up a watchlist for stocks of interest so they never miss an opportunity to buy or sell. This documentation is for users new to buying and selling stocks on Meritrade. This guide walks you through creating an individual account on the Meritrade platform.

Click on Create account​ An image showing where to click Create an account The Login button is for users with an existing account on the app. Important Please use an email address that has never been used to create an account on Meritrade, if not the system will flag it. In addition, your password must contain 8 characters consisting of an uppercase letter, a lowercase letter, a number, and a special character. Select Individual​ An image showing where to select Individual to open an individual account On this page, two options are available to you: Individual — select this if you intend to buy and sell stocks on a personal basis. Do you have an existing CHN Number? — tick Yes or No. If Yes, enter your CHN. Log into your Meritrade account​ An image showing the Log in page Enter your email address and password to log in to your Meritrade account. Important Each funding transaction attracts a 1% processing fee, capped at ₦300. This means that for every amount you fund your account with, 1% is deducted as a fee, but if that 1% exceeds ₦300, only ₦300 will be deducted regardless. Click on Add money​ An image showing the location of Add Money There are two ways to fund your account: Through bank transfer: An image showing the account number to copy and bank name to transfer money to Copy the displayed account number and perform the transaction in your bank app. You will receive emails from Paystack and Meristem, and your funds will be reflected in your account shortly. You will also receive emails from Paystack and Meristem, and your funds will reflect in your account within a short period.

Meritrade is an online stock trading app owned and controlled by Meristem, used to buy and sell stocks on the Nigerian stock exchange, provide up-to-date market insights, and let users set up a watchlist for stocks of interest so they never miss an opportunity to buy or sell. This guide walks you through the steps required to sell your stock(s) on Meritrade.
documents.s: Overview (definition of the app, audience, purpose of this guide)

documents.t: A Meritrade account. Internet connectivity. A list of stock tickers/names to sell.

Log in to your Meritrade account​ An image showing the Log in page Enter your email address and password to log in to your Meritrade account. Click on New Trade​ An image showing the location of New Trade on homepage Select Sell​ An image showing the location of Sell Click on Select Stock​ An image showing the search bar to be used to locate stock tickers An image showing the list of stocks that you own so you can the ones you want to put up for sell Only the stocks you have bought previously will show up; select the ones you want to sell. Enter the quantity of stock you want to sell​ An image showing where you indicate the quantity of stocks you want to buy As you enter the quantity of stock you want to sell, the price is reflected. Click on Select portfolio​ An image showing where you select your portfolio When you created your Meritrade account, you were automatically assigned a portfolio. Select Order Type​ An image showing the different order types There are two types of orders: Market: this is an instruction to sell the stock immediately at the best price available. Select this order if you want to ensure the stock sells, regardless of price. Limit: this is an instruction to sell only if the price gets to a certain level specified by you. Select this order when you want a stock only if it is sold at a specific price entered by you. Important Be mindful of when you plan to sell your stock(s); try to sell when the market is still open. If you sell your stock(s) after the market closes or before it opens, kindly note that you will only be able to place a limit order. Select Order Term​ An image showing where to select Order Term This tells those selling your stock(s) for you how long your order is valid for. For example, if you give a limit order and you set 1 day as your order term, if after 1 day, your stock is not sold at the price you wanted, then by the end of the day your order becomes invalid. Click on Preview Order​ An image showing where to click to preview your order An image showing the preview Preview your order to ensure everything is correct. You also see the additional cost that comes with selling stocks, such as broker commission and regulatory fees. Click on SELL​ An image showing the SELL button Once you click on SELL, you will receive a copy of your trade order and a contract note in your email linked to your Meritrade account. Click on Back to home​ An image showing that your order was successful Once the order has been successfully placed, you will see a message saying, Trade Order Placed Successfully, then click Back to home. In addition, once your stock is successfully sold, it will be reflected in your available balance, and you will be notified through SMS as well.

These are the rules I used to keep the four Meritrade guides consistent and clear.

Use # for the document title, ### for main steps and top-level sections (Overview, Prerequisites), and #### for nested sub-steps within a main step. Order matters? Number it, Order doesn't matter? Bullet it. If the reader has to do things in sequence, use a numbered list. If they're choosing between two equal options (like Market Order vs. Limit Order), use bullets. Callouts keep the > on every line, not just the first one. If your important note is two lines, both lines start with >. Two kinds of callouts, two jobs. [!NOTE] is for background info that doesn't change what the reader does. [!IMPORTANT] is for anything that actually changes what they need to do. The command or instruction for a step lives in the step heading only. Body text underneath describes confirmation or context, and never repeats the command or instruction for the same action.

All images for a project live in one parent-level folder, with a subfolder per guide. No guide gets its own separate top-level folder. File names: first word starts with a capital letter, then the rest is lowercase, hyphens, no parentheses. Parentheses can actually break how Markdown reads the image path, not just look messy. Alt text and caption say the same thing, always. Write the description once, use it both places. Two images in one step should have their own captions. Never make one caption cover two or more screenshots. Caption(s) should be italicized and bold. Images come before the step explanation.

A period after a backtick only if it's really the end of a sentence. A step heading is a title, not a sentence; it never gets a period, backtick, or anything. If a backticked word genuinely ends a real sentence, it gets its period like anything else would. Backticks should match exactly what's on screen. Don't sneak your own words in there. If the screen says "Funding request is being processed," that's what goes in the backticks, not "Funding request is being processed message." "And," not "&." Spell it out in body text. Hyphenate number + unit. "4-digit PIN," not "4 digit pin." And once you pick how PIN is capitalized, keep it that way everywhere, not just in the heading.

Check every prerequisite against every path in the guide. If something's only needed for one method (like a bank card only mattering for card payments, not bank transfer), say so. Don't list it as required for everyone if it isn't. Read for meaning, not just grammar. A sentence can be perfectly correct and still be wrong for the guide it's in, like a buying guide accidentally saying "sell" because it got copied from somewhere else. Ask "does this actually match what I'm teaching here," not just "is this sentence okay."
Use "stocks" consistently, not "shares." Pick one term for the thing being bought and sold, and use it everywhere across a guide (and across guides).

Save with the extension from day one. .md, not added later. VS Code, GitHub, and Google Drive all need it to know what they're looking at. File and folder names follow the same capitalization: first word capitalized, rest lowercase, hyphens between words (e.g., Buying-stocks-on-meritrade.md). This is the standard convention across every guide and image file. Spell brand names the way the company spells them. Meritrade, not meritrade. Note Every rule here came from a real issue I caught while editing my own guides. I used Claude to help organize, phrase, and refine them into this document.

My name is Chinenye Precious Anyasor, and I have a bachelor's in human physiology. By now, I thought I would be working in a lab somewhere, but alas, life had its plans. Before I developed an interest in tech documentation, I spent two years as a human resources professional in very fast-paced environments, at a YC-backed fintech and a large BPO. There, I was told that my superpowers are process ownership and the ability to pick up new tech with ease. Those skills tie neatly into tech documentation. Personally, I have been off social media for the past six months, learning the trade secrets of tech documentation. What I did not expect was the tunnel vision and focus that came with it. Now I cannot decide whether or not to go back. I love reading, cliché, right? But I do. Mostly fiction nowadays; I used to read history and autobiography. Since I started learning tech documentation, I have taken several technical communication courses and put what I learned into practice. I wrote a set of getting started guides for a stock-trading app, covering how to create an account, fund it, buy stocks, and sell stocks. I added an FAQ page, a style guide, and a case study explaining how I approached the work. I also built this portfolio website myself with Docusaurus, and I write technical explainers and personal essays on my blog. I have wanted to travel for the longest time to Spain, Italy, France, and Thailand — you know, places with history. Anyway, I am fun, super collaborative, and a terrific researcher. I can work remotely, and I have a strong itch to get undeniably good at writing documentation.
These are the tools I used to write, design, and publish my portfolio.
Markdown: the format I used to write my guides. VS Code: my editor for writing and building this site. Google Docs and Microsoft Word: document drafting and review.
Git and GitHub: version control for my work. Docusaurus: the documentation framework this portfolio is built on.
Greenshot: screenshots. Lucidchart: diagrams. Canva: the design of my homepage banner.
Claude: an AI assistant I used while building this portfolio.
